question: The tennis class is “for beginners”. Who is it for?
choices: People who teach the sport.
People who are learning to play.
People who win a lot of games.
People who only want to watch.
note: A beginner is new to a sport. A coach teaches it.

picture.alt: A tennis racket and yellow ball.

question: At the sports centre, someone asks, “Where’s the changing room?” What do they want to do?
choices: Put on their sports clothes.
Pay for another class.
Get a different class time.
Give back their tennis racket.
note: People use a changing room to put on different clothes. To change a class time, ask at the desk.

question: Eda says, “I’ll book a court for Friday.” What is she going to do?
choices: Buy their tickets to watch a match.
Find a book about playing tennis.
Ask a coach to teach them on Friday.
Keep a place for them to play.
note: Booking a court means choosing a time and keeping the court for your game.

picture.alt: A tennis racket and yellow ball.

question: At the desk you hear, “The six o’clock class is fully booked.” What does that mean?
choices: The class has already finished.
You can pay when you get there.
Every place in the class is taken.
Everyone in the class has a book.
note: “Fully booked” means all the places are taken. A class can be fully booked days before it starts.

question: The coach says, “No need to book. Just drop in on Tuesday.” What can you do?
choices: Ask the coach to come to your home.
Go to the class without booking first.
Book your place before Tuesday.
Only watch the class this week.
note: “Drop in” means come along. The coach is saying you can turn up without making a booking.

picture.alt: A clock beside a blank calendar.

question: The swimming lesson starts at four. Your bus leaves at five. What do you ask before you book?
choices: What time does the lesson finish?
Can I leave the lesson early if I need to?
Could you tell me what time it starts?
Is there a later lesson I could join?
note: You know when it starts. The finish time tells you if you can stay for the whole lesson and catch your bus.

picture.alt: A clock beside a blank calendar.

question: A sign says “Tennis: £12”. You and a friend want to play. The sign doesn’t say if both of you must pay £12. What do you ask?
choices: Can I pay my £12 by card?
How much is tennis, please?
Is it cheaper to play in the morning?
Is that £12 each or £12 for the court?
note: The sign already gives a price. Asking “each or for the court?” tells the worker exactly which part is unclear.

question: At your first tennis lesson everyone has a racket. Yours is at home. You’d like to use one just for the lesson. What do you ask?
choices: Do you sell tennis rackets here?
Could I watch the others today?
Could I borrow a racket for today?
Could I come back with my racket tomorrow?
note: Buying a racket makes sense if you want to keep it. You only need to borrow one until the lesson ends.

picture.alt: A tennis racket and yellow ball.

question: You arrive for football practice. Two groups are playing. You know your coach’s name, but you can’t see him. What do you ask at the desk?
choices: Could you call my coach for me?
Where does Coach Ali’s group play?
Can I wait here until a coach comes over?
Where do people play football here?
note: Both groups play football. The coach’s name helps the staff send you to the right group.

question: A judo course lasts two months. You’ve never tried judo and want to try one lesson before you pay for the course. What do you ask?
choices: Can I try one class first?
Can I pay for the course in two parts?
Can I watch one class first?
Can I speak to someone who takes the class?
note: Watching can help you decide, too. “Can I try one class?” asks to get on the mat and do judo yourself.

picture.alt: A folded martial-arts jacket and belt.

question: At the pool a teacher asks, “Can you swim?” You can swim a little, but you still need lessons. What do you say?
choices: Could I watch a lesson before I join?
I’d like some swimming lessons, please.
I’d prefer to start with the easiest class.
A little. Which class is good for me?
note: “I’d like some swimming lessons” explains why you’re there. “A little” also tells the teacher what you can do, so they can suggest a class.

picture.alt: A pool beneath a rocky opening.

question: Your sister is twelve. She wants to come to a cycling class with you. The advert doesn’t give an age. What do you ask?
choices: Can I bring my sister to watch?
Do you have any classes for children?
Can a twelve-year-old join this class?
Could I book two places for this class?
note: Watching and joining are different. Giving her age lets the staff say whether she can ride with the class.

picture.alt: A bicycle and a pink cycling jersey.

question: You’re going to your first indoor sports class. You have football boots and running shoes. What do you ask the coach?
choices: Can I leave my outdoor shoes at the desk?
Which shoes should I wear indoors?
Can I buy sports shoes at the centre?
Should I bring both pairs with me?
note: Taking both might help on the day. “Which shoes should I wear?” asks the coach to choose the right pair now.

question: You have your keys and money with you at the gym. You want to leave them somewhere safe while you play. What do you ask?
choices: Is there a locker I can use?
Could you watch my things during the game?
Is there a table where I can leave my things?
Can I keep my bag beside the court?
note: You can leave things on a table, but anyone can pick them up. A locker keeps them safe while you play.

question: You’re the coach. One player asks, “Can I join now?” The game has started, but there’s a space in the next game. What do you say?
choices: Would you like to watch from here?
Sorry, this game has already started.
Could you come back at the same time tomorrow?
This one’s started. You can play in the next one.
note: “This game has already started” explains the wait. Adding “You can play in the next one” offers the place that is available.
